disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the prediabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is between 5.7% and 6.4%, the range used for prediabetes. This is a common and often reversible stage where lifestyle changes make the biggest difference.

summary: Your HbA1c of 5.7% falls in the prediabetes range, which means your blood sugar is a bit higher than typical but not in the diabetes range. Along with your weight being above the healthy range and your blood pressure and cholesterol conditions, this means it's a good time to focus on prevention. The most valuable next steps are keeping up with your lipid profile, kidney function, and blood pressure checks, staying regularly active, and following the food guidance around sodium, saturated fat, and fibre. These steps together can help support healthier blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels over time.

risk_factors.label: Body weight above the healthy range
Existing health condition: High blood pressure
Existing health condition: High cholesterol or triglycerides

comorbidity_assessment.note: Blood pressure and blood sugar often influence each other, and both can affect your heart and kidneys over time, so keeping sodium low and staying active supports both.
Elevated cholesterol or triglycerides can add to cardiovascular risk alongside higher blood sugar, which is why the fibre-rich, low-saturated-fat diet pattern is especially helpful for you.

constraints: Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day (about one teaspoon of salt in total); avoid pickles, papad, instant noodles and salty snacks.
Follow a DASH-style pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses and low-fat dairy (or fortified alternatives).
Keep saturated fat low (limit ghee, butter, coconut oil, red and processed meat); avoid trans fats (vanaspati, many fried and bakery foods).
Include soluble fibre daily (oats, barley, pulses, psyllium) and unsaturated fats (nuts, seeds, olive or mustard oil in small amounts).

foods_to_eat: Leafy greens like spinach and kale
Whole grains such as oats, barley and quinoa
Fatty fish like salmon (limited to twice a week)
Fresh fruit such as berries and apples
foods_to_avoid: Refined flour products like white bread and pastries
Deep-fried and bakery foods with trans fats
Canned soups and instant noodles high in sodium
Salted snacks like chips and crackers
Full-fat dairy products like butter and cream
plan.portion_guidance: Aim for balanced plates: half filled with vegetables, a quarter with whole grains or starchy vegetables, and a quarter with lean protein. Use small amounts of healthy fats like olive oil for cooking or dressing. Keep portions moderate to fit the 1,200 kcal target, using household measures like cups, katoris or handfuls as a guide.
plan.hydration: Drink about 8 cups of water through the day. Herbal teas and infused water with lemon or cucumber are good options. Limit sugary drinks and caffeinated beverages with added sugar.
based_on: high cholesterol: low saturated fat, DASH-style pattern
soluble fibre and unsaturated fats emphasis

exercise: Start with 20-30 minute sessions of moderate aerobic activity, like brisk walking, swimming, or cycling, 4-5 days a week, working up toward 150 minutes a week over the coming weeks.
Add simple muscle-strengthening activities, such as light resistance bands or bodyweight exercises, on 2 non-consecutive days a week.
Because regular moderate aerobic activity helps lower blood pressure and improves HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, try to keep your sessions consistent rather than occasional.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with 15-20 minutes of walking a day, 5 days a week, and gradually build up to 30 minutes a day, 5-6 days a week as your fitness improves.
lifestyle.weight_management: Since your BMI falls in the overweight category, gentle, steady weight loss through regular activity and balanced meals can help improve your HbA1c, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels over time. Aim for gradual, sustainable changes rather than quick fixes.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, limit screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet to support restful sleep.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5-10 minutes a day to help calm your nervous system, which can also support healthy blood pressure.
Try a short daily mindfulness or relaxation practice, such as guided meditation or gentle stretching, to help manage everyday stress.
Consider regular walks outdoors, which combine physical activity with a calming change of scenery.
behaviour_change: Keep a simple log of your activity and meals to help notice patterns and celebrate small wins.
Since you don't currently smoke, keep up this healthy choice as it supports your heart and blood vessel health.
Build activity into daily routines, like taking stairs or parking farther away, to make movement a natural habit.
Check in with your progress every few weeks and adjust your goals gradually rather than making big changes all at once.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Catches progression from prediabetes to diabetes early.

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

preventive_actions: Keep track of your blood pressure at home on a regular schedule.
Follow the DASH-style eating pattern with plenty of vegetables, fruit, pulses, and low-fat dairy.
Limit sodium to under 2,300 mg a day by avoiding salty snacks, pickles, and processed foods.
Add soluble fibre like oats, barley, and pulses to your daily meals.
Aim for regular moderate aerobic activity most days of the week, since it can help both blood pressure and cholesterol.
Keep your scheduled lipid profile and kidney function tests so your care team can track changes over time.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
